nameStory: The "rough-winged" part of this swallow's name comes from the tiny serrations along the edge of its wing feathers that you can only feel if you handle the bird up close. These microscopic hooks feel like the fine teeth of a saw, giving the wings their distinctively rough texture that sets them apart from other smooth-winged swallows.
description: The Northern Rough-winged Swallow is a small, brownish swallow that's less flashy than many of its relatives. About 5-6 inches long, it has a plain brown back, white belly, and distinctive dusky throat that lacks the crisp white found on similar swallows. These aerial acrobats spend most of their time swooping and diving through the air to catch flying insects, rarely landing except to rest or nest.

idTips.label: Dusky throat
idTips.description: The throat appears grayish-brown or dusky, not bright white like many other swallows - this shadowy throat patch is visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Plain brown upperparts
idTips.description: The back and wings are a uniform brownish color without the metallic blue-green sheen of tree swallows or the rusty patches of cliff swallows

idTips.label: White belly
idTips.description: The underparts are clean white, contrasting with the dusky throat in a way that creates a subtle two-toned appearance below

idTips.label: Slightly notched tail
idTips.description: The tail has a shallow fork or notch, less dramatic than a barn swallow's deeply forked tail but more noticeable than a tree swallow's square tail

idTips.label: Erratic flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, jerky movements and sudden direction changes as it snaps up insects, often flying lower over water than other swallows

habitat: Look for Northern Rough-winged Swallows near water sources like rivers, streams, ponds, and lakes throughout New England's lowlands and valleys. They prefer areas with exposed banks, cliffs, or human-made structures like bridges and culverts where they can excavate nesting burrows. You'll often spot them flying low over water surfaces where insects are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in New England in late April to early May, when you'll see them hawking insects over newly ice-free waters and beginning to excavate nesting burrows in sandy banks.
seasonality.summer: Most active and visible during breeding season, constantly flying back and forth to feed nestlings hidden in burrows. Listen for their soft, buzzy calls near nesting colonies.
seasonality.fall: Gathers in small flocks before migration in August and September, often mixing with other swallow species as they prepare for their journey south.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England, having migrated to Central and South America where flying insects remain abundant year-round.

funFact: Northern Rough-winged Swallows are nature's recyclers - they often take over old kingfisher burrows or even nest in drainpipes and culverts, but the most surprising nests have been found inside the hollowed-out bodies of old cars abandoned near riverbanks!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Bank Swallows, but Bank Swallows have a distinct dark breast band across their white chest, while Rough-wings have that dusky throat fading to white. Memory trick: "Rough-wings are rough around the throat, Bank Swallows wear a chest band like a belt."
compareHints: Northern Rough-winged Swallows are the only rough-winged swallow species in New England, making them unique in their genus here. Compared to other New England swallows, they're the plainest - lacking the metallic colors of Tree Swallows, the rusty rump of Cliff Swallows, the deeply forked tail of Barn Swallows, and the crisp breast band of Bank Swallows. Think of them as the "plain brown bird" of the swallow family.
